opener.heading: Week 33: Pretend Passport World Adventure 🌍
about: On Friday morning Azlyn makes a passport out of four sheets of paper and a cereal box, and it takes one stamp a day until Thursday. Each day lands somewhere new: a doorstep covered in colored flour, a hallway full of paper planes, a canal running down the patio, a hot pan and flat bread, a market on the rug. The passport is the thread that ties them together. She carries it, stamps it, and reads it back through on the last night.

Most of this comes out of the recycling, the spice rack and the jar of saved bottle caps, so the shopping is smaller than the list below looks. The two hottest afternoons are water. No holiday falls in this range, which leaves swimming on Tuesday and the library on Wednesday as the only fixed points in the week.
azlyn: Changing one thing at a time. She adds a paperclip to a paper plane, throws again, and gets an answer she can use.
Numbers attached to something she wants. Bottle-cap coins marked 1, 2 and 5, prices on the stock, and change to hand back.
Where water goes and why. She tapes a leaking join, raises the top end of the channel, and watches a cork follow the slope.
Pressing, folding and pouring with two hands. Dough under a dinner plate, napkin layers pulled up one at a time, tea poured from as high as she can hold the pot.
That waiting buys her something. Colored salt sits in clean stripes if she stops between each layer, and turns gray if she hurries.
you: Sensory bottles work as a calming tool, and it's worth keeping one
Making the material is part of the activity
Changing one thing at a time is real experimental method
Water play is unusually complete developmental work
Effort makes food taste better, and that's a measurable effect
Shop play is the most efficient math practice available at three
Distinct layers only form if you wait, and that's a visible lesson
shopping: An empty cereal box, plus 2 sheets of thick card
A stapler and a glue stick
Adult scissors and a table knife (adult only)
Washable poster paint, or an ink pad
Colored chalks, 6, plus a fat stick for the sidewalk
Ground turmeric, paprika, and cocoa or ground coffee
Food coloring, blue and one other
Tomatoes, cilantro or basil, and 1 green chile
Rice, 1 tbsp, or sequins or small beads
For the sinking test: 1 grape, 1 dried pea, 1 coin, 1 lego brick, 1 cork and 1 bottle cap
1 clear plastic bottle, 16 oz, lid on
Bottle caps, 20–30, saved in a jar
Clean jam jars, 2, at least one with a lid
Cups you don't mind syrup in, 4
A mixing bowl and a dishpan
A pitcher, and a watering can or bucket
A funnel, or cut the top off a spare bottle
A teapot, or a pitcher with a spout
A tin or small bowl for the coins
Dinner plates, 3 (two for the press, one for the stack)
A teaspoon, a spoon, a fork and a wooden spoon
1 large box Azlyn can sit in, plus a cardboard tube and cardboard offcuts
A small suitcase or bag, and a shopping bag
A paddling pool, or a big storage box
Dish towels, 3, one you don't mind crayon on
An old towel to kneel on, plus towels for the water days
A sheet or bath towel for the awning, and 2 clothespins
1 small toy and 1 book she can pack
A loose photo of Azlyn, if you have one
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 14 months this week. He scribbles, stacks two blocks and knocks them down again, and has three to five words he uses on purpose. He walks well enough to fetch a paper plane off the hall floor and carry it back to her.

days.prepTonight: Four sheets of printer paper, an empty cereal box, the stapler, the glue stick and a potato on the kitchen table, plus a small photo of Azlyn if you have one loose.

opening.title: The Photo for the Front Page
opening.need: 1 sheet of printer paper · pencils or crayons · her photo, if you found one · 1 permanent marker · the cereal box.
steps: Ask her for a picture of her own face for the front of the passport. Name the parts out loud while she draws.
Ask which country she wants to go to first. Take whatever she says, made-up ones included, and write it across the top.
Set the drawing and the photo beside the cereal box. Tell her the passport gets built at 9:15.

main.title: The Passport That Gets Stamped
materials: 1 cereal box, or a sheet of thick card, for the cover
Her photo, or her drawing of her face from 8:00
Washable poster paint, or an ink pad
steps: Fold the four sheets in half and stack them inside each other. She folds and presses every crease with her thumb.
Cut the front panel off the cereal box, fold it round the stack and staple twice through the fold. Both tools stay in your hands.
Glue her drawing or photo onto the first inside page. Write PASSPORT, her name and her age on the cover.
Number the pages 1 to 7 in the corners, one for each day of the week. She holds it open while you write.
Cut the potato in half and carve a shape into the flat face: a star, a circle, the letter A. She stands back and you say why.
Fold the paper towels into a pad and soak it with paint, or open the ink pad. She stamps page one and says the country out loud.
main.tip: Let her stamp page one four or five times. A passport covered in the same star beats one tidy print.

outside.title: The World Drawn on the Path
paras: Chalk the world onto the sidewalk. One long blob for the sea, then a country wherever she points, names written in. Walk from one to the next counting the steps, then hop the route back. August has been dry, so it will still be there on Thursday.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and presses hard enough now to see his own mark appear. Give him a folded sheet and a fat crayon at the far end of the table while the stapler is out. Outside, a stub of chalk and a patch of sidewalk to himself.

second.title: The Bottle for the Long Journey
second.intro: Every traveler packs a bag. Hers gets a bottle with the sea in it, and the case shuts before dinner.
materials: 1 clear plastic bottle, 16 oz, lid on, label peeled off
4 tbsp cooking oil (or clear glitter glue if you have it)
1 tbsp rice, sequins or small beads
steps: Let her peel the last of the label off.
Fill the bottle two-thirds with warm water at the sink. The oil beads rounder in warm water.
Two drops of blue coloring, lid on, one hard shake. Stop at two or you lose the light through it.
Pinch the rice, sequins or beads in a few at a time. Sweep the misses up before you put Kreston down.
Pour the oil in until a finger's depth sits on top, then screw the lid down hard.
Wrap packing tape round the lid three full turns, over the threads, so it cannot come off in anyone's hands.
Turn it over together and watch. Then pack the case: passport, bottle, one toy, one book, and stand it by the front door.
second.tip: Name it tonight and keep it somewhere she can reach on her own.

alternatives: One bottle, water and food coloring, and skip the oil.
Pack the case with clothes she chooses and nothing else.
Draw the seven country pages instead of stamping them.
Line every bottle in the house up by size.
outAgain: Playgroup, with the passport in her bag and one stamp in it
A friend's house, if anyone has the paddling pool up
The shaded end of the park after four, once the slide has cooled
The store for popsicles, eaten on the wall outside

aroundWorld.title: The Color of the Cover 🛂
paras: Passports come in four colors and no more. Burgundy across most of Europe, green across much of the Muslim world and West Africa, blue across the Americas, black in a few countries including Botswana and New Zealand. The choice tends to say which neighbors a country stands with.
aroundWorld.tryIt: One new food on the table for each country in her passport. Flatbread on Tuesday, mint tea on Wednesday, rice with turmeric through it tonight. She stamps the page after she eats it.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The reigning British monarch travels without a passport, because British passports are issued in his name. Japan's Emperor and Empress go without one too.

days.krestonPM: At 14 months he wants that bottle and will get it in the end, so hand it over on your terms with your hands round his. Then give him the small bag to carry up and down the hall, loading and unloading. He works at it for five minutes, wanders off and comes back to it all afternoon.

insight.headline: Sensory bottles work as a calming tool, and it's worth keeping one.
paras: Azlyn will turn that bottle over a hundred times this week. The oil and water separate at a pace her eyes can follow, slower than anything else in the room, and watching something move at that speed pulls her breathing down with it. Occupational therapists hand these out for a living. Keep this one somewhere she can reach on her own, because a tool she fetches herself does more than one you produce at the point of a meltdown. Offer it before the storm rather than during, on the drive home or before dinner, and she starts to notice what it does for her.

days.safety: The table knife for the potato stamp is adult-only, and so are the scissors and the stapler. All three go back on a high shelf between uses. Kreston at 14 months will grab the bottle and swing it, so tape the lid all the way round, and keep rice, beads and staples off the floor. An hour of chalking a sidewalk in August is an hour in full sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Colors on the Doorstep
days.prepTonight: Flour, turmeric, paprika and cocoa out on the counter with four small bowls and a spoon, and a big empty box by the back door for this afternoon.

opening.title: Turmeric, Paprika, Cocoa, Flour
opening.need: all-purpose flour · ground turmeric · paprika · cocoa or ground coffee · 4 small bowls · 1 spoon.
steps: Four bowls on the table, a heap of flour in each. The first stays white, and she uses it most.
Spoon a little turmeric into the second, paprika into the third, cocoa into the fourth. She stirs each until the color goes through.
Smell all four. Everything goes to the front step, bowls at your height, and she washes her hands before touching her face.

main.title: The Rangoli at the Front Door
materials: All-purpose flour, 4 cups, as the white and the base
Your phone, for the photo before it goes
Her passport, for the stamp on page two
steps: Sweep the step and test one hidden corner with a pinch of turmeric. If it stains the stone, move the whole thing onto the path.
Chalk a circle the size of a dinner plate, then six petals round it. Draw the first two and hand her the chalk.
She fills each petal by pinching powder out of the bowl and letting it fall. Show her the pinch once.
Top up any bowl that runs low with flour and another spoonful of turmeric, paprika or cocoa. The yellow goes first, every time.
Kneel her on the old towel for the middle so she can reach in without walking through her own work.

Photograph it from standing height, then pour the pitcher over it together and brush it into the drain. Dry her hands, press one thumb into what is left in the turmeric bowl and stamp page two of the passport. She says the country out loud.
main.tip: Tell her at the start that it gets washed away before dinner. Say it once and she will pour the water herself.

outside.title: Six Petals Chalked on the Path
paras: Same shape, out on the path and big enough to walk on. She chalks the circle first, then six petals round it, and fills each one solid with a different color. Work the shaded stretch and move out as the sun comes round. She walks the ring at the end, one petal at a time, naming the color under her feet.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and takes powder by the handful, so he gets all-purpose flour and nothing with spice in it. He will pat it, drag a finger through it and put a white hand on the door. Outside, sit him on the towel at the edge of the path with four clean bowls out of the cabinet to stack and knock over.

second.title: The Elephant Big Enough to Sit On
second.intro: The doorstep patterns end up on a blanket across an elephant's back, and the elephant is a box she can sit in.
materials: 1 large box she can sit in or straddle
1 cardboard tube, or a rolled-up cereal box, for the trunk
steps: Stand the box up and fold the top flaps out so she can climb in and out without help.
Tape the tube onto the front, low down, and leave it loose enough to swing.
Fold two offcuts in half and tape one to each side of the head end for ears. The fold makes them stand out and saves cutting.
Marker in her hand: two eyes above the trunk. She decides how big, and they will be enormous.
Crayons or paint on the sides, whatever she wants on them.
Dish towel flat on the floor, and she draws the six-petal pattern on it in crayon. As many as fit.
Lay the towel over the box, tie it underneath with string, cushions in, and she rides.
second.tip: Sit down inside it with her once, even if you barely fit. Fifteen minutes in there beats an hour decorating the outside.

alternatives: Blanket over the sofa arm, cushions underneath, and call that the elephant.
Paint the box one color and stop there.
Draw on the dish towel only, and hang it in the window.
Line up every soft toy in the house and give them all a ride.
outAgain: A bus ride to nowhere in particular, the front seats right behind the driver
The park with a bottle of water each, shade side only
A walk to the ice cream shop and back the long way
The garden with the sprinkler on, if nobody can face leaving
A drive with the windows down and one stop for a look at something
days.krestonPM: At 14 months he stacks two blocks and knocks them down, so give him the offcuts and let him build beside the elephant. He will want in the box with Azlyn. Let him once she has had it to herself, and stay down at their level.

insight.headline: Making the material is part of the activity.
paras: Shop-bought colored sand would have got her to the doorstep forty minutes sooner and taught her nothing. Azlyn stirred turmeric into flour and watched white turn yellow in a bowl she was holding, which is chemistry she can feel in her wrists. She works longer with a material she made herself, and the preparation carries as much of the learning as the finished picture. It also buys you a morning out of one bag of flour and three jars from the back of the cabinet. Any time a project has a prep step you could do the night before, hand it to her instead.

days.safety: Paprika and turmeric sting hard in eyes, and Kreston at 14 months takes powder by the handful. Keep the bowls at adult height, hand Azlyn one color at a time, and wash hands before anyone rubs a face. Turmeric stains stone and grout, so test one hidden corner of the step first. Whole chalks and chalk stubs are choking size at 14 months, so the chalk box stays up on the step with you. Kreston works four clean bowls out of the cabinet, because the color bowls stay up on the step until she rinses them at four. The step and the path are both in full sun by ten, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Long Flight
days.prepTonight: Clear the hallway floor end to end, count six paperclips into a saucer, and stack twenty sheets of printer paper with the masking tape at one end of it.

schedule.label: Get Outside

schedule.label: Her Job

opening.title: The First Plane Off the Table
steps: Fold one plane in front of her, whichever fold your hands remember. Say each step out loud as you make it.
Give her a sheet and let her fold her own however she wants. Leave it alone. A plane folded wrong flies wrong.
Write 1 and 2 on the wings and throw both off the end of the table. Tell her the hallway opens at 9:15.

main.title: One Change, Then Race Again
materials: Masking tape for the throwing line and the landing marks
1 tape measure, or a length of string
The hallway, or the longest room in the house
steps: Tape a line across the floor at one end. Toes stay behind it on every throw, hers and yours.
Fold three planes the same way and number them 1, 2 and 3. Hers from 8:00 can race later.
Throw plane 1. Tape a short strip where the nose lands and write 1 on it. Throw twice more from the same spot and keep the furthest mark.
Change one thing on plane 2 and one thing only: a paperclip pushed onto the nose. Throw, mark, number.
Plane 3 gets a different single change: bend the back edge of both wings down a fingernail's width. Throw, mark, number.
Measure from the line to each tape mark and lay the three planes beside their own marks. She calls the winner.
main.tip: Mark where the nose lands, not where the plane stops. A plane that skids another few feet down the hall has stopped flying, and she will argue it.

outside.title: Launching From the Top of the Slide
paras: Take three planes and a spare to the playground before the heat sets in. Height is the change she cannot make indoors. She climbs the ladder, you stand at the bottom, and she throws from the top of the slide instead of coming down. One will end up on a roof.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and walks well enough to be the retriever: he fetches a plane, carries it back while walking, and hands it over. He will crumple one on the way. Give him his own sheet to crush and drop.

second.title: The Airport in the Hallway
second.intro: Chairs in two rows, a shoebox that beeps, and a line. Azlyn checks in the case she packed on Friday and hunts for her seat number.
materials: Her passport from Friday (or 4 sheets folded and stapled, stapler in your hands, if it has gone missing)
steps: Two lines of masking tape down the hallway for the aisle. Chairs in two rows inside them, facing the same way, seat numbers on tape stuck to the backs.
Shoebox at the top of the hall. The suitcase goes in one end and out the other, and you make the noise.
Passport open at page three. Draw a stamp with the marker and say the country out loud as you press.
Write a name and seat number on each of the four boarding passes: hers, yours, Kreston's, and the toy in the case.
She matches her number to a chair and sits. Do not point at the right one.
Trolley: tray, paper cups, dish towel over your arm. She serves the row one cup at a time and takes them back in.
Landing. Everyone leans to one side, the case comes back out of the scanner, and she carries it to the front door.
second.tip: Take the smallest role going, passenger rather than pilot. She runs a better airport when the adult in it takes instructions.

alternatives: Two chairs and a dish towel. Same flight, ten minutes.
Boarding passes only, drawn and handed out to the house.
Pack and unpack the case four times and call it a stopover.
Draw the view from her seat.
outAgain: Scooter or balance bike, on the flat stretch by the stores
The big-slide playground, for more launching
A long walk with the stroller and something cold in it
The park with a picnic blanket and whatever is in the fridge
Water fight in the yard, if the afternoon has gone loud
days.krestonPM: Give him a chair in the second row, a paper cup and a boarding pass to chew. At 14 months he has three to five words and will use one on the cup. He would rather work the shoebox end than sit, so let him.

insight.headline: Changing one thing at a time is real experimental method.
paras: Azlyn wants the paperclip, the bent wings and a longer nose all on the same plane, and the plane that comes back tells her nothing. Hold her to one change per throw and she gets an answer she can use. Scientists call this controlling the variables, and a three-year-old runs it on a hallway floor with paper and a strip of tape. She will not name the method and does not need to. She keeps the habit of changing one thing, looking, then changing the next, and it turns up later over a jammed zip and a tower that keeps falling.

days.safety: Paperclips are the size Kreston chokes on. Count them out of the saucer at the start and all six back in before he goes down, and sweep the throwing lane with your hand, not your eyes. The saucer stays up on the windowsill between throws. She throws from the top of the slide with you standing at the bottom of it and nobody on the steps below her. Hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, because a playground before eleven is still forty-five minutes of August sun.

days.title: The City Built on Water
days.prepTonight: Cut six to eight large plastic bottles in half lengthways tonight, so she wakes up to a stack of channels and you are not holding a knife at nine.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Bottles Laid End to End

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Following the Water to the Drain

opening.title: The Bottles Laid End to End
opening.need: the cut bottles · packing tape · the back step.
steps: Carry them out two at a time and lay them end to end down the patio, overlapping each by a hand's width.
Ask her which end should be at the top. Prop that end on the back step and let her look down the line.
Tape the first two together while she holds them steady. Leave the rest of the joins for 9:15.

main.title: The Water Runs Downhill
materials: 6–8 large plastic bottles, cut lengthways (adult, done the night before)
Corks, bottle caps and 2 foil trays cut into boats
steps: Tape every join with the upper bottle inside the lower one. Water runs out of any join taped the other way round.
Dishpan at the bottom of the run, under the last bottle.
First pitcher of water. Watch the whole length, mark every leak with a finger, then tape those joins again with her.
Chalk the numbers 1 to 5 along the channel, so she has something to shout when a cork sticks at four.
Race the cargo: a cork, a bottle cap, a foil tray boat. She pours, she calls the winner, she fishes them out.
Finish with the watering can tipped in at the top for a flood, then empty the bowl over the flower bed and dry the step.
main.tip: Steeper is not always faster. Let her raise the top end onto a second step and watch the cork jump the channel.

outside.title: Following the Water to the Drain
paras: She already knows where it goes, because a leaf went down that drain in July. Today she calls it before it happens. Stand her at the top of the driveway with a full bottle and have her chalk two crosses on the slope, one where she thinks the water will stall and one where she thinks it will pick up again. Then pour, and walk it down to the drain checking her marks against the water. The grit catches it in a place she never guessed.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and water is the best thing in the garden. Sit on the step beside him with one shallow tray, an inch deep, and a jar lid to float. You stay within arm's reach the whole time and the tray goes over the moment you stand up.

second.title: The Gondolas on the Lagoon
second.intro: The paddling pool is the lagoon and the wooden spoon is the pole. Azlyn poles boats across it until one goes under.
materials: Paddling pool, or a big storage box filled with water
3 foil tray boats from this morning, or 3 fresh foil trays
1 wooden spoon, or a straight stick, for the pole
Pebbles, bottle caps and small toys as cargo
1 funnel, or a cut-off bottle neck
Her passport, for the stamp on page four
steps: Fill the pool with a few inches of tepid water. Sun hats on before anyone gets in.
Float all three boats and let her push them about before the poling starts.
Wooden spoon as the pole. Show her the push against the bottom of the pool once, then leave her to it.
Load one boat with pebbles, bottle caps and small toys, one at a time, counting out loud, until it goes under. Say the number it sank on.
Funnel into the second boat, pitcher of water through it, and she watches it sit lower without sinking.
Race two boats the length of the pool, one hand poling each.
Tip the pool out the moment she is done, wrap her in a towel, and stand the boats on the windowsill to dry. Passport open at page four, a wet thumb pressed onto it, and she says the country out loud.
second.tip: Use tepid water. Hose water in August comes out colder than it looks, and a cold pool ends the afternoon in four minutes.

alternatives: Dishpan on the grass, three boats, nothing else.
Sink the boats on purpose and count what it takes.
Pour from pitcher to pitcher to bottle and back, and call it the canal.
Wash every bottle cap in a bowl of bubbles and line them up to dry.
outAgain: The riverside path, counting the boats and the bridges
The duck pond, with the last of the heat off the day
The park in the shade, if she has had enough water for one day
A walk to look at every drain cover on the street
The garden with the hose on a trickle
days.krestonPM: He is never beside the pool, the bowl or the bucket without you within arm's reach. Give him a job on dry ground: a dishpan with an inch in it, three jar lids too wide for his mouth, and room to drop them in from standing. At 14 months he carries things while walking, so he will fetch you pebbles all afternoon.

insight.headline: Water play is unusually complete developmental work.
paras: The hour you block out for that canal runs more through Azlyn than most of what you could buy her. She is pouring, which is wrist control and forward planning, and judging how much a pitcher holds against how much the channel takes. She watches a cork go where the water goes and works out why one join leaks and the next does not. Add the talk coming out of her while she does it and you have covered fine motor, physics, early math and vocabulary in one wet morning. She works it in bursts of twenty minutes and comes back to it, which she does for no toy that has batteries in it.

days.safety: A 14-month-old drowns in an inch of water and it happens without a sound. Kreston is never beside the pool, the bowl or the bucket unless you are within arm's reach, and every container gets tipped out the moment you stop using it. Cut bottle edges are sharp, so run a strip of tape along any edge she will hold, or fold the lip over, before she carries the first one out. A wet patio is slippery, so shoes on or bare feet, never socks. The driveway feeds a gutter on a live road, so Kreston is in the stroller with the brake on from the moment you leave the gate. At the drain the stroller stays back from the curb with the grating on your side of it, and you stay between Azlyn and the road for the whole walk down. Hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Corks, bottle caps and pebbles are all choking-sized for a 14-month-old down on the same ground fetching things, so the cargo comes out of a bowl in your hand and goes back into it the moment a boat sinks or a race ends.

days.title: Hot Pan, Flat Bread
days.prepTonight: Flour, salt, a mixing bowl and two dinner plates out with the parchment paper, and an avocado somewhere warm to ripen for lunch.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Tortilla Press Made of Two Plates

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Picking What Goes in the Salsa

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Laying the Flowers Down the Table

schedule.label: Wind-Down

opening.title: Warm Water Into the Flour
opening.need: 2 cups masa harina or all-purpose flour · a pinch of salt · 1 cup warm water · 1 mixing bowl · 1 dish towel.
steps: Flour and salt into the bowl. She stirs with her hand, so she knows what dry feels like before it changes.
Pour the warm water in a little at a time while she mixes. Stop when it holds together and comes off the sides.
Knead it into one ball between you, thirty seconds each. Dish towel over the bowl while she washes her hands. It wants half an hour.

main.title: The Tortilla Press Made of Two Plates
materials: 2 cups masa harina, or all-purpose flour
1 dry frying pan (adult at the stovetop)
1 dish towel to keep the stack warm
Her passport, for the stamp on page five
steps: Roll the rested dough into walnut-sized balls. She rolls and counts, and one will come out enormous and need splitting.
Tear two squares of parchment paper. One flat on a dinner plate, a ball in the middle, the second square on top.
Second plate on top, and she presses down with both hands and all her weight. Peel the paper back and look.
Pan on a medium heat, dry, no oil. Forty-five seconds a side, and it puffs in the middle when it is done. You stay at the stovetop throughout.
Stack them on the plate under the dish towel.

Wash the mixing bowl and hand it back. Avocado in, lime squeezed over, and she mashes while you cook the last two. Keep one raw ball back on the counter under an upturned bowl for four o'clock. Passport out before lunch, a floury thumb on page five, and she says the country out loud.
main.tip: The first three will be thick and crack at the edges. She eats those, and by ball eight her pressing has sorted itself out.

outside.title: Picking What Goes in the Salsa
paras: Mid-August is the week the tomatoes come all at once, so raid what you have: the pots by the back door, the community garden, a neighbor's glut, the cheap boxes at the market. She picks by squeezing. Add cilantro or basil. She can carry one green chile in its bag, not in her hand.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and works with his whole palm, so give him one piece of dough on his chair tray, pressed flat and wider than his fist, to pat and pull at. He stays out of the kitchen while the pan is on.

second.title: Napkin Flowers for the Table
second.intro: A folded napkin looks like nothing until the layers come up one at a time. A slow ninety minutes that ends with something down the middle of the table.
materials: 1 packet of paper napkins, or paper towels
Food coloring in a saucer of water, for dipping the edges
steps: Stack six napkins square and fold the whole stack into a concertina, folds a finger wide. She folds, you keep it lined up.
Tie string tight round the middle and knot it twice. She holds a finger on the knot while you pull.
Trim both ends into rounds or points. She says which shape, you cut, and the scissors go back on the shelf.
Dip each end into the colored water for two seconds and set it on the draining board. The color creeps up while she watches.
Pull the layers up one at a time, from the middle outward. Slow hands. A torn layer stays torn, and she will tear two.
Write a country on the tied middle of each flower, one for each day of her passport week.
Stand the best one in the jam jar with an inch of water and lay the rest down the middle of the table.
second.tip: Make one alongside hers and tear a layer on purpose. She needs to see an adult wreck one and carry on.

alternatives: Paper towels instead of napkins, no color, no string.
Dip folded paper in color and open it flat, no flower.
Fold the concertinas into fans and use them, because it is hot.
Lay the table for seven and name a country at every place.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coolest room in town today
The splash pad, if the pool is booked out with the summer-break crowd
The park sprinklers, with a change of clothes
A shaded café, if nobody can face a changing room
The paddling pool at home, tipped out after
days.krestonPM: He goes to the pool too. At 14 months he walks the steps into the shallow end holding your two fingers, which he could not do in the spring. Twenty minutes, then out and dry before he goes cold. Azlyn hands him his towel.

insight.headline: Effort makes food taste better, and that's a measurable effect.
paras: Azlyn will eat a tortilla she pressed herself and turn down the same tortilla off a plate, and she is not being difficult. Researchers have put numbers on this: people rate food they helped make higher than identical food handed to them, and the effect grows with the work that went in. For a three-year-old sorting out what she does and does not eat, that lever beats any amount of encouragement across a table. Give her the pressing, the stacking and the mashing. She sits down to lunch already invested in it, and the argument you were braced for never starts.

days.safety: The stovetop and the dry pan are adult-only, and the pan stays hot long after it comes off the heat. Turn the handle inward, keep Kreston out of the kitchen, and let each tortilla sit a minute before she picks it up. A walnut-sized ball of raw masa is throat-sized at 14 months, so the rolled balls stay up on the counter, the one held back for four o'clock included, and his piece goes onto the tray flattened wider than his fist. The scissors stay with you. Chile on fingers goes into eyes and stays there, so the chile stays in its bag until you cut it, and hands get washed before anyone rubs a face. Picking is done in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Market Day
days.prepTonight: Tip the jar of saved bottle caps into a bowl on the table, put a sheet and two clothespins beside it, and stand the teapot out for this afternoon.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Pouring the Tea From High Up

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Carrying the Tray to the Sink

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the New Library Book

opening.title: Coins Made From Bottle Caps
opening.need: 20–30 bottle caps · 1 permanent marker · 1 tin or bowl.
steps: Tip the caps out and let her sort them into three piles her own way, by color, size, whatever she picks.
Write 1 on every cap in the first pile, 2 on the second, 5 on the third. She names the number as you write it.
Count them into the tin out loud, one at a time. Tell her that is all the money in the house today.

main.title: The Souk on the Rug
materials: 1 low table, or an upturned box
1 sheet or bath towel for the awning
1 tin or bowl for the money
Dish towels, scarves, fruit, tins and toys as stock
Her passport, and a dab of poster paint or the ink pad
steps: Rug down on the floor, low table or upturned box at the back. She sits behind, customers stand in front.
Stand the two chairs behind the stall and clip the sheet across their backs so it hangs over her. Shade matters at a market and she will feel it.
Send her round the house for stock. Take what she comes back with, shoes and remote control included, and lay it in rows.
Price everything 1, 2 or 5 on the torn tickets. She decides what is expensive, and a tin of beans at 5 with a teddy at 1 is her market.
Coins to the customer, tin to the seller. You shop, she sells, and you hand over the exact tops the ticket asks for.

Buy again with too many coins so she has to give some back, then fill the shopping bag and let her count what is left. Last purchase of the morning is a stamp: she presses a bottle cap into the paint, prints page six of the passport and says the country out loud.
main.tip: Overpay on purpose at least twice. Catching you beats any sum she gets right, and she will check every customer after the first.

outside.title: Walking Only in the Shade
paras: One rule for the whole walk: her feet never touch sun. She picks the route, crossing the road where the shade crosses, waiting under a tree for a cloud, hopping the gap where a driveway breaks the line. Put a hand flat on a sunny wall and then a shaded one.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months with three to five words, and the stall suits the ones he has. He takes things off it and walks away with them, which is trade as far as he is concerned. Hand him one item and a jar lid too wide for his mouth as his coin, and see whether he swaps. The bottle caps and the clothespins stay out of his reach all morning.

second.title: Pouring the Tea From High Up
second.intro: Everyone sits on the floor round a tray for this one, and the pour is the whole skill.
materials: 1 teapot, or a pitcher with a spout
4 clear plastic cups, never glass, because the high pour is designed to miss
A plate of cookies or dates
steps: Cushions on the floor in a circle, tray in the middle, shoes off. Nobody sits on a chair for the next hour.
She tears the mint leaves into the pot, or drops the two teabags in. Torn leaves smell more than whole ones.
One teaspoon of sugar, then hand-warm water from the tap. Never hot, and check it on the inside of your wrist before it goes near her.
Pour one cupful and tip it back into the pot. Do it twice. Mixing by pouring is how the tea gets made.
Now the high pour. Cup on the tray, and she lifts the pot as high as she can and aims. The dish towel is for what happens next.
Once she lands one, she serves the room: a cup to each person, carried in two hands.
Cookies or dates on the plate in the middle, and nobody gets up until they are gone.
second.tip: Half a cupful in the pot, no more, while she is learning the height. A pot light enough for her to lift saves ten spills.

alternatives: Cold mint water in a pitcher, poured outside, no pot at all.
Set the tray up as a tea shop and sell the tea from the stall.
Pour water between cups at the sink until she has had enough.
Cushions, cookies and a book, and skip the tea.
outAgain: The library, the every two weeks one, and a book set somewhere far away
Indoor playground, if the library is packed with the summer-break crowd
The store, and let her pay for one thing with real coins
The park, late, when the grass has cooled off
A friend's garden, with the tea things in a bag
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him in the board book corner while Azlyn chooses. At 14 months he pulls books off the shelf faster than you can put them back, so give him a small pile of his own on the floor. He gets his own cup on the cushions later.

insight.headline: Shop play is the most efficient math practice available at three.
paras: Azlyn takes two bottle caps for something she has priced 2, then hands one back when you pay with three. Inside twenty minutes at that stall she has counted, matched a number to a quantity, compared 1 against 5, sorted stock into rows and worked out that four coins beat two. None of it looks like math to her. Number sense at three grows out of handling real quantities with a reason attached, and the stall supplies the reason. Let her charge you 5 for a shoe and pay it without arguing, then come back and pay wrong on purpose.

days.safety: Bottle-cap coins and clothespins are both choking size, and Kreston is at floor level all morning. Count the caps out of the tin at the start and count them back in when the stall comes down, and keep the two pegs on the sheet where you can see them. He never gets a bottle cap to hold, even as a customer, because they go in the mouth inside four seconds at 14 months. Use plastic cups for the high pour rather than glass, and check the tea water on the inside of your wrist before it goes on the tray. Hand-warm, never hot. The shade walk still has gaps in it, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Last Stamp
days.prepTonight: Corn syrup, dish soap, oil and food coloring out with four cups, and find the tall straight glass and a clean jam jar with a lid.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Which Cup Goes to the Bottom

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Three Photographs a Visitor Would Take

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, and the Passport Read Back Through

opening.title: Which Cup Goes to the Bottom
opening.need: 4 cups · corn syrup or honey · dish soap · water with blue food coloring · cooking oil.
steps: Fill each cup a third full, one liquid in each. Let her tip the syrup in and take her time.
Line the four up and ask her to put them in the order she thinks they will stack, heaviest at the bottom.
Leave her order on the table as she set it. Tell her you find out at 9:15 whether she has it right.

main.title: The Glass With Four Floors
materials: 1 tall straight glass, or a clear bottle with the top cut off
Water with blue food coloring in it
A grape, a bottle cap, a lego brick, a cork, a dried pea and a coin
steps: Corn syrup straight into the bottom of the glass from the cup, one steady line down the middle. It should not touch the sides.
Hold the teaspoon against the inside of the glass, back of the bowl facing up, and pour the dish soap onto it so it runs down the wall.
Same again with the blue water, then the oil. Her hands on the cup, your hand on the spoon.
Leave it alone for five full minutes. Wash the cups together, stand them back in the order she picked at 8:00, and come back to four clean floors.
Drop the six things in one at a time. Before each one she guesses which floor it will stop on.

Look at where they land. The grape sits on the syrup, the coin goes to the bottom, the lego brick will surprise her. Then stand the glass beside her line-up from 8:00 and read the floors against her order, top to bottom. She sees for herself how much of it she called.
main.tip: The spoon is what makes this work. Poured straight in, the layers churn into one brown glass with no second try.

outside.title: Three Photographs a Visitor Would Take
paras: Walk the street as if you had landed this morning and never seen it. She gets three photographs on your phone and no more. Late August light on the brick, the mailbox, a front garden gone wild. Look at all three on the way back and ask what she would tell a visitor.

days.infant: Kreston is 14 months and everything on that table is choking size, so he is not at it. Once she has read the floors against her line-up, give him the four cups: he stacks two, knocks them down and starts again, which he could not do in June. On the walk he wants out of the stroller, so allow twice the time.

second.title: One Layer for Every Country
second.intro: Seven stripes in a jar, one for each day she has stamped, and the last goes in tonight. It takes the whole afternoon and her hands are in it throughout.
materials: 1 clean jam jar with a lid
1 sheet of paper rolled into a funnel
Her passport, for the last stamp
steps: Two big spoonfuls of salt into each bowl. The rest stays in the bag for the seventh layer.
One chalk per bowl. She rubs it against the salt round the side until the color goes through. A few minutes a bowl.
Roll the sheet of paper into a funnel and hold the point in the neck of the jar.
Spoon one color through the funnel. Stop. Tap the jar on the table until the layer sits flat, and let her look before the next goes in.
Repeat for all six, stopping between each. Any hurry mixes two colors into mud.
Last layer plain white salt from the bag, for today, and the lid on tight.
Sticky label on the front with her name, the date and the seven countries, then draw the last stamp in the passport with the marker.
second.tip: Tilt the jar as she pours and the layer lands at a slope. Do it for two of the six.

alternatives: Three colors instead of six, and a smaller jar.
Colored salt in a tray to draw in with a finger, no jar.
Rub the chalk into salt and fill the jar tomorrow.
Read the passport back through, page by page, and stop.
outAgain: The grocery store, and she picks one thing from a country she stamped
The park, with the shopping under the stroller
The bakery for something for the morning
A walk to post a picture of the jar to whoever cares
The garden with the sprinkler on
days.krestonPM: Salt is not for him at 14 months, so he gets the spoon and the jar lid on the floor beside the table. He is scribbling now, so paper and a fat crayon buy ten minutes. In the store, one thing to hold to the register and hand over himself.

insight.headline: Distinct layers only form if you wait, and that's a visible lesson.
paras: Pour the salt fast and the colors churn into one gray band. Stop between each one, let it settle, tap it flat, and she gets seven clean stripes she can count back through her week. Azlyn is three, and waiting is the hardest instruction in the house, so a jar that shows her what the waiting bought beats being told to be patient. The glass this morning made the same argument on a longer clock. Keep the jar on the windowsill. She built the argument out of salt and chalk, and she will make it back to you the next time something has to sit.

days.safety: The grape, the coin, the lego brick and the dried pea are all choking size and Kreston will be under that table. Keep them in your pocket between drops and count all six back in. Nothing in the glass gets drunk, dish soap least of all, and the glass goes on a high shelf after. The walk down the street runs in late-August sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.
